newsitem.title: PERU: Peru opens police trial for hostage crisis lapse.
newsitem.headline: Peru opens police trial for hostage crisis lapse.

text.p: Peru's highest military court began proceedings on Wednesday against 26 police officers blamed for the security lapse that enabled Marxist rebels to seize the Japanese ambassador's home for four months.
The Supreme Council of Military Justice took testimony from two police colonels and will continue processing the rest in coming days, court officials said.

The policemen -- including five generals, two of whom were held hostage by the rebels -- are being tried for negligence and disobedience. They allegedly ignored intelligence warnings and failed to provide proper security at the Dec. 17 Japanese embassy's cocktail party.

Fourteen Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels burst into the reception, initially taking more than 500 people hostage. They held on to 72 of their captives for 126 days before the April 22 military storming of the ambassador's residence, which safely freed all but one of the hostages.
All the rebels, one hostage and two policemen died in the battle.

The highest-ranking policemen held responsible for the security lapse, Lt.-Gen. Luis Malasquez, in charge of Lima police, has left for Mexico and risks being extradited if he does not return to face trial, the court officials said.
His daughter, Giuliani Malasquez, said, however, that her father was merely taking a holiday and "is going to present himself at the due moment."

Last week Interior Minister Gen. Cesar Saucedo said the National Intelligence Service and the armed forces were free from blame for the MRTA raid, which saw much of Peru's security forces' top brass taken captive. But he pledged to punish the police officers held responsible.
